title: Arctic Circle: Line of the Midnight Sun
description: Explore the Arctic Circle — the latitude of the midnight sun crossing eight countries, from Norway to Alaska, and slowly drifting. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Reykjavík sits 268.7 km south of the Arctic Circle — close enough that Iceland's June nights never truly darken, even though only tiny Grímsey island touches the line itself.
quick_answer: The Arctic Circle is the line at 66.5633 degrees north latitude where the Sun can stay in the sky for a full 24 hours at the June solstice. This page maps where the circle runs and explains the midnight sun it governs.

Highways cross the line with signs and visitor stops (Finland's at Rovaniemi is the famous one) — the map shows every crossing a road can reach.
Light, not cold, is the circle's real curriculum: school terms, festivals and building design all bend around the light calendar.
Tromsø (69.65°N) lies 343 km north of the circle, deep enough for a geometric midnight-sun run from about May 23 to July 22 — and the polar-night stretch to match.
Rovaniemi, Finland markets itself as the Arctic Circle town — the line runs through its Santa Claus Village, which is why the crossing ceremony happens indoors-adjacent to reindeer.

popular_table.note: The line's latitude (66.5633°N) is set by Earth's current axial tilt and drifts ~15 m a year — signs planted decades ago now stand slightly off the true line.

faq: How many people live inside the circle?
Roughly four million across the eight countries — the Arctic is inhabited homeland, not empty wilderness, with Tromsø and Murmansk among its cities.
When is the midnight sun at the circle itself?
One night a year in theory (the solstice), stretched to a few by refraction and the Sun's width — the higher you go, the longer the run.
Yes, in several countries: Finland's Highway 4 at Rovaniemi, Norway's E6 near the Saltfjellet pass, Alaska's Dalton Highway and Canada's Dempster all cross it.
Iceland's mainland tops out just short of the line; only Grímsey, an island 40 km offshore, is crossed — Iceland is the circle's 'nearly' country.
What is polar night like in towns?
Not full darkness at inhabited latitudes: midday brings a few hours of deep blue twilight near the solstice, which residents plan their outdoor time around.
Does the circle pass through the North Pole's ice cap?
The pole is 2,600 km north of the circle — the cap's edge varies with sea ice, but the circle itself crosses the Arctic Ocean's waters between Greenland and Russia.
The auroral oval hovers near (not on) the circle — its towns are prime aurora territory precisely because their winters are long and dark at the edges.
